what_it_does: This paper describes an extremely precise measurement circuit for reading capacitive sensors (devices that sense pressure, proximity, or humidity by measuring how much electrical charge can be stored in a tiny gap). The challenge: thermal noise (random jiggling of electrons caused by heat) corrupts the measurement, especially when the circuit tries to read quickly. The solution combines two noise-reduction tricks: chopping (rapidly swapping the measurement signal back and forth to distinguish real signals from noise patterns) and a lead-compensation technique (like a prediction layer) that keeps the measurement loop stable without requiring power-hungry amplifiers. The circuit achieves extremely high precision (8.7 attofarads—about one-thousandth of the charge stored on a single atomic nucleus) with a figure-of-merit 185.2 dB, making it suitable for sensitive sensor applications.
